children: Americans' anger with fraud in the job search is reaching a fever pitch. Now, LinkedIn is rolling out new tools to help users figure out what is real-and avoid handing over money or their résumés to scammers.

The new levers, which the company plans to release this month, focus on verification, a system through which users can submit government identification and their professional email addresses. In turn, their profiles display a check mark, giving it a sign of authenticity.

The company says it stops tens of millions of fake members who could scam users by posing as recruiters. Still, some slip through the cracks. As profiled by The Wall Street Journal this week, a Chicago man who calls himself The Profiler has flagged thousands, warning users to scrutinize even verified accounts.

The LinkedIn update fills a hole that scammers have used to wrest job seekers' data and sometimes their cash. Some scammers list themselves as employees of companies where they have never worked. A desperate job seeker might not fact-check that affiliation and, thrilled to be contacted by the purported recruiter, send over her résumé or pay for consulting services to improve her chances at getting a job.

With the new feature, LinkedIn says, the administrators of verified company pages can also prevent those users from appearing in search results as their employees. Users who are flagged by a company as impostors would now have seven days instead of a longer period to prove they actually work at an organization before being removed.

This tightens an existing practice: In some cases now, profiles that are reported as improperly affiliated with a company have a 14-day window to update their accounts or appeal, screenshots seen by The Wall Street Journal show.

In another new initiative, some companies will be able to pre-emptively require verification for anyone who claims to be affiliated with their company. Another update will allow colleagues and classmates to fact-check one another's résumés, which LinkedIn said would offer additional credibility.

Oscar Rodriguez, LinkedIn's vice president of trust product, told the Journal this month that scammers adapt quickly to the platform's defensive efforts and that anti-spam efforts are a constant battle. He said verification offered additional context but wasn't a guarantee.
